extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and describes criteria for valid scientific induction, the proper use of explanations vs descriptions, and the correct application of causal language as discussed in a classical philosophy-of-science text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity as condition of valid induction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a condition of the validity of every induction that there be uniformity in the course of nature (the Law of Causation); but it is not necessary that the uniformity should pervade all nature — it suffices that it pervades the particular class of phenomena to which the induction relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An induction concerning planetary motions or magnetic properties is not invalidated by supposing weather is irregular, provided the relevant phenomena are under general laws. This avoids demanding universality of law across all phenomena in early science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction implies a general fact either known or now knowable
rubrics_metrics.description: Every induction by which we infer any truth implies either that the general fact of uniformity is already known, or that we may now know it from the evidence at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep distinct whether an induction rests on previously established generalization or is itself establishing that general truth from instances (e.g., 'the Duke of Wellington is mortal' implies either general mortality already known or is now inferred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific inference must pass through a general proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, the inference must necessarily pass through the intermediate stage of a general proposition, because Science wants its conclusions for record, and not for instantaneous use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical inferences made for immediate guidance may match scientific reasoning in intellectual quality, but for science proper conclusions need to be formulated as general propositions for documentation and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Description from Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different descriptions (modes of representing phenomena) are not the same as different explanations (accounts positing mechanisms or agents); a description may be compatible with multiple explanations, but explanations that assert different real mechanisms can be mutually incompatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kepler’s law as a description could coexist with different mechanism-explanations; but a vortex theory (asserting real vortices) and Newtonian gravitation (asserting a universal centripetal law) are incompatible as explanations because they posit different physical agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses as representation vs hypotheses as factual claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hypothesis is merely a mode of representing the facts (a Description), it may be reconcilable with other theories; if it asserts a material agent or mechanism (an Explanation), it becomes a factual claim that can be true or false and may contradict other explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating theories, determine whether the hypothesis is intended as a representational aid or as a literal claim about physical agents — this affects whether apparent contradictions are real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting predictions indicate incompatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If two theories make different predictions about the same phenomenon (e.g., differing predicted return periods for a comet), they cannot both be right; conflicting predictions show genuine incompatibility between explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical prediction as a decisive test: contradictory forecasts cannot both be true; examples include historical disputes about voyages, steam navigation, and astronomical returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'cause' depends on communicative necessity, not only 'active force'
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary language we often call that antecedent a 'cause' which is the one condition the hearer may need to be informed of; we are inclined to name as cause the condition whose specification supplies the information otherwise missing, rather than every antecedent condition or the element exerting active force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish proximate vs remote causes and positive vs negative conditions: calling the sentinel's absence 'the cause' is justified because it supplies the informative element, whereas saying 'possession of bodily organs' as cause of death is usually unhelpful unless that is the doubtful factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative or preventive conditions may be treated as causes when informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative conditions (absence of something) or preventive properties can be spoken of as causes when they are the informative factor that explains the effect, e.g., 'died for want of medical advice' or 'drowned because he could not swim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formula that bundles all negative conditions into 'absence of counteracting causes' can account for preventive properties; in practice, we call a negative condition a cause when it is the pertinent, non-implied factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes and apparent exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of Composition of Causes (that multiple causes combine) is generally fulfilled, but apparent exceptions arise when attention is paid to remote instead of immediate effects (e.g., one spark suffices to explode a barrel; two sparks don't seem 'more effectual').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve apparent counterexamples by identifying immediate collocations: duplicating causes may double the collocation (and hence the immediate effect), but the remote or bounded nature of some effects (dose thresholds, saturation) can make duplication not increase the observed outcome in the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive properties as special cases of absence of counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some properties appear purely preventive (e.g., opacity intercepting light), which at first glance seem exceptions to composition laws, but they can be treated as agencies that defeat another agency rather than producing effects by the same law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if opacity functions only by defeating light passage, one can still include such negative conditions within the general causal scheme by treating them as absences or counteracting agencies; these need not undermine practical application of causal formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human will and moral causation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a disputed case whether human volitions are exempt from causal laws; the view defended here is that if a person's actions invariably conform to his character, and a perfectly informed observer could predict them, then human actions fall under causal regularity similarly to physical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating moral or human sciences, avoid assuming a metaphysical exception for will; analyse predictability relative to character and circumstances rather than appealing solely to consciousness of freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad induction arises from improper interpretation of coincidences and prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Beliefs founded on coincidences or preconceived a priori prejudices (e.g., sowing seed during moon increase) are instances of induction but bad induction; the supposed evidence of experience is necessary to their hold on the mind yet may be misinterpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine inductive support from coincidental or prejudiced inferences; evaluate the strength of experiential evidence and antecedent probability to avoid accepting spurious generalizations.
